references.text: Uses the same Hebrew word וַיִּנָּחֶם (vayinnachem) for God as 'repents' or 'changes his mind' regarding his action.
Samuel says that the Lord repented that he had made Saul king, using the same Hebrew root word נחם.
Presents an apparent contradiction by stating that the Glory of Israel does not lie or repent, balancing the understanding of God's 'repentance'.
God saw their deeds and repented (וַיִּנָּחֶם) of the evil he had said he would do to them.
The Lord says that he may repent of the disaster he planned to bring upon them if they turn from their ways.
Promise that the Lord will repent of the evil he spoke against his people if they improve their ways.
Example where the Lord repented of the evil he had spoken against his people, referring to King Hezekiah.
God's principle of repenting of the disaster he planned to bring upon a people who turn from their wickedness.
Amos prays for Jacob, and the Lord repents: 'It shall not be,' says the Lord.
The Lord repents again after Amos' intercession: 'This also shall not be,' says the Lord God.
Similar situation where Moses intercedes for the people, and the Lord forgives them in response to Moses' prayer.
Moses recounts how he prayed for the people and the Lord listened to him during the incident of the golden calf.
Poetic description of how Moses stood in the gap for the people to turn away God's wrath.

Both verses illustrate the Lord's reaction toward his people; while Exodus shows that wrath can be turned into grace, Psalm 106 shows how that same wrath leads to abhorrence when the people's sin is persistent.
Illuminates the same theological principle: God's wrath turns to compassion and protection for His people.
